Talking with others about the event or its aftermath

Memory.value: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.
When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief

vignette:
Amina, a 25-year-old nurse from an African immigrant family, had been working long shifts in a city hospital when she first found herself back in the war zone where she had spent part of her early adulthood, helping in a field clinic during a period of fighting. The traumatic day she kept returning to was one in which the sounds of shelling moved closer than anyone expected, the clinic shook, and people she had been trying to care for were suddenly lying on the floor while she was forced to crouch behind a metal cart and listen to the screams in the corridor. In the middle of that chaos, she had felt exposed and powerless, and what stayed with her was not only the terror of the event but the sense that she had not been able to protect anyone. After she returned to the United States, the memory began to intrude in fragments at work, especially in the emergency unit when monitors beeped sharply or when a patient's sudden cry cut through the room. When the memory returned, Amina said it was not like thinking about something that had happened before; it felt as if she were back there again, with the same urgency in her body, and the grief that came with it could become so heavy that she had to stop whatever she was doing and leave the room. That overwhelm made her more likely to push the experience away entirely, and she became skilled at cutting off any thought that might open the door to it. She would drift into a world of her own while charting, stare through conversations with colleagues, and deliberately avoid talking about the war with her partner, even when he asked why she seemed distant.

What made this pattern harder to break was the meaning Amina had come to attach to what happened. She had become convinced that the fact she was still alive, while others had suffered and died, meant something was fundamentally wrong with her. She felt permanently humiliated by how frightened she had been, as if a real nurse should have been braver, calmer, more useful. In her mind, the clinic scene replayed not only as horror but as evidence that she was inadequate and defective, and that shame made it feel unsafe to turn toward the memory for too long. The more those thoughts of humiliation and defectiveness settled in, the more determined she became to escape from them. She would lose herself in daydreams on the commute home, scroll mindlessly in bed, or keep herself busy with extra shifts, anything to avoid sitting with the image of the corridor, the dust, and the sense of failure that seemed to follow it. Even in brief moments of quiet, if the memory surfaced, she would experience it as vividly present and feel the grief all over again, which only strengthened her sense that there was something broken in her and that she could not bear to examine it directly.

Over the months, avoiding the memory began to narrow her life. At work, Amina stayed efficient and professional on the surface, but she made sure never to linger in conversations about trauma, and she withdrew from coworkers who talked about difficult cases over coffee. At home, her partner noticed she was physically present but often unreachable, slipping into silence or seeming to float away when he tried to ask about her days. She knew he cared, but she feared that if she spoke about the war she would be overwhelmed by the same flooding grief and shame, and that he would see the inadequacy she believed was there. There were evenings when she sat on the sofa and allowed herself to drift into fantasies of being somewhere else entirely, somewhere without sirens or the smell of dust and antiseptic, because that felt easier than letting the images in. Yet the more she stepped away from the memory, the less controlled it felt when it returned; it arrived more like a living scene than a recollection, and each return seemed to confirm the harsh verdict she had already reached about herself. By the time she sought help, her distress had become hard to contain. She came because the episodes of reliving were becoming too frequent to manage at work, and because she was frightened that she would keep disappearing into avoidance and distance, losing her relationship and the part of herself that once felt capable. What she most hoped for was relief from the shame and grief that clung to the memory, and what she most feared was that the event had indeed revealed something permanently wrong with her.
